sql_schemas: table leave_requests | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, start_date, end_date, requested_days, reason, status, approver_id, approval_comment, submitted_at, decided_at, cancelled_by, cancelled_at | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code; approver_id -> employees.id; cancelled_by -> employees.id | indexes: status: the approvals queue filters SUBMITTED requests awaiting a decision; employee_id: the queue scopes to the manager's direct reports (employee_id = ANY(...)); (leave_type_code, start_date): existing list/date-range filtering

table employees | fields: id, employee_number, first_name, last_name, email, password_hash, role, manager_id, department, hire_date, termination_date, employment_status | pk: id | fks: manager_id -> employees.id | indexes: manager_id: resolves a manager's direct reports for queue scoping; email: unique lookup for login/profile; employee_number: unique lookup
data_notes:
This feature is a web/ (frontend) change only and introduces NO new persistence. The approvals queue reads the existing backend GET /leaves (role-scoped to the manager's direct reports) and reuses the existing approveLeave/rejectLeave api-client methods; no new tables, columns, or repositories are added, and the backend/API contract is untouched per the feature constraints.

The two tables saved above (leave_requests, employees) are PRE-EXISTING backend tables, referenced by name only — they are unchanged by this feature and their schemas already live in the backend architecture (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md). They are listed here solely to document the read surface the queue depends on:
- leave_requests.status = SUBMITTED is the queue filter; employee_id scopes to the manager's direct reports (the backend GET /leaves already applies this role scoping).
- employees.role (MANAGER/ADMIN) and employees.manager_id drive link visibility and the route guard; role comes from GET /employees/me (EmployeeProfile), never from decoding the JWT in the browser.

No repository interfaces are introduced: the web layer's data-access boundary is the existing IApiClient/ApiClient (backed by HTTP fetch, not PostgreSQL), and the existing LeaveService/EmployeeService delegate to it. The queue reuses getLeaves(), approveLeave(), rejectLeave(), and getAvailableLeaveActions() — no new transport methods.

No new persistent state means no transaction contract is needed: the queue is read-only, and each approve/reject is a single existing API write (the backend owns its own unit-of-work for those transitions).
transaction_contract: EMPTY — this feature introduces no multi-step writes in the web layer. The queue is read-only (GET /leaves), and each approve/reject is a single existing API call (approveLeave/rejectLeave) whose atomicity is owned by the backend service, not the web layer. No caller-controlled transaction boundary is required.
